title: 10 Appliance Repair PPC Tips to Book More Calls
html:
Appliance repair PPC works best when each appliance gets its own campaign, junk searches are blocked on day one and every call is tracked. Those three moves protect your budget before you spend much of it.

Appliance repair PPC pays when someone with a broken fridge, washer or oven searches and finds you first. It loses money when your ads show for parts, manuals and repair videos. These tips fix the waste first, then improve the ads.

What are the 10 best appliance repair PPC tips at a glance?

The 10 tips below are sorted by speed to first booked calls, fastest first. Use the table to pick three, then read the entries for the steps.

#TipCostSpeed to first booked callsDifficulty
1Build one campaign per applianceAd spendFirst weekEasy
2Add negative keywords on day oneFree (your time)First weekEasy
3Track phone calls as conversionsFree (your time)First weekMedium
4Set the budget from your job valueAd spendFirst weekEasy
5Name the appliance in every adFree (your time)First monthEasy
6Send each ad to a matching pageFree (your time)First monthMedium
7Run ads only when someone can answerFree (your time)First monthEasy
8Read the search terms report weeklyFree (your time)OngoingMedium
9Watch the three Quality Score partsFree (your time)OngoingMedium
10Add Local Services Ads beside searchAd spendOngoingHard

Which appliance repair PPC tips work in the first week?

Four setup tips work in week one: split campaigns by appliance, block junk searches, track calls and set a budget from your job value.

1. Build one campaign per appliance

Give refrigerators, washers, dryers, ovens and dishwashers their own campaigns. Separate campaigns let you set a budget and write ads for each appliance.

  • List the appliances you repair well and the ones you decline.
  • Start with the two most profitable appliances, not all of them.
  • Group keywords by appliance, such as "refrigerator repair" and "fridge not cooling".

Numbers: ad spend, first week. Example (sample split): one campaign for refrigerator repair and one for washer repair. Mistake to avoid: one campaign for every appliance, so a cheap dryer click eats the refrigerator budget.

2. Add negative keywords on day one

Block searches from people who want parts, manuals or repair videos before you spend. Google says negative keywords help ads reach people more likely to want what you offer.

  • Use phrase or exact match for the words you block. Google notes that negatives do not match close variants.
  • Add the singular and plural forms yourself, since Google does not.
  • Add terms slowly. Google warns that too many negatives can reduce your reach.

Numbers: free, first week. Example (sample list): manual, parts, diy, jobs, training, free. Mistake to avoid: blocking a word that real customers also use, such as "near me".

3. Track phone calls as conversions

Count phone calls as conversions so you can see which ads make the phone ring. Google explains that call tracking shows which keywords and ads led to calls. A call counts only if it lasts longer than a length you set.

  • Set a minimum call length that filters out wrong numbers.
  • Place the Google tag and phone snippet on every page that shows your number.
  • Test with one real click before you trust the numbers.

Numbers: free, first week. Example (sample rule): count calls longer than a short minimum you pick, then adjust after a week of listening to recordings. Mistake to avoid: counting every ring as a lead.

4. Set the budget from your job value

Work backward from what a booked repair is worth to you, then set the daily budget. A budget picked at random will either starve the campaign or burn cash.

  • Write down your average repair ticket and your target cost per booked job.
  • Divide your monthly ad budget by that target to see how many jobs it must book.
  • Check the maths again after the first month of real data.

Numbers: ad spend, first week. Example: a $2,000 monthly budget with a $200 target means 10 booked jobs. Mistake to avoid: judging by clicks.

Which appliance repair PPC tips pay off in the first month?

Three ad tips pay off in month one. Name the appliance, send clicks to a matching page and run ads only when your phone is staffed.

5. Name the appliance in every ad

Put the appliance and the problem in the first headline. A person with a warm freezer wants to see the word freezer.

  • Use the same words as the keyword group.
  • Add your town and one trust detail you can prove, such as licensed and insured.
  • Promise only what you can deliver, such as a quick callback.

Numbers: free, first month. Example (sample headline): "Refrigerator Not Cooling? Call a Local Repair Tech". Mistake to avoid: promising a same-day visit you cannot always keep.

6. Send each ad to a matching page

Send the click to a page about that appliance, with the phone number at the top. A visitor who lands on a general home page often leaves.

Numbers: free, first month. Example (sample page): a washer repair page with common error symptoms, your service area and a call button. Mistake to avoid: sending every ad to the home page.

7. Run ads only when someone can answer

Schedule ads for the hours your phone is staffed. A paid click that reaches voicemail is the most expensive click you can buy.

  • List the hours someone reliably picks up.
  • Set an ad schedule to match those hours.
  • Add a missed call text-back if your tools allow it.

Numbers: free, first month. Example (sample rule): if nobody answers after early evening, stop the ads then and restart them at opening. Mistake to avoid: running ads overnight with no callback plan.

Should an appliance repair company run search ads or Local Services Ads first?

Most appliance repair companies should start with search ads, then add Local Services Ads once calls are tracked. Search gives you control over keywords and pages. Local Services Ads give you a verified panel and pay-per-lead calls.

Organic rankings reduce what you pay per call over time, so appliance repair SEO belongs in the plan. Compare all Google Ads management options before you choose.

Which appliance repair PPC mistakes waste the most budget?

The costliest mistake is paying for clicks that never become calls, which comes from broad keywords, missing negatives or a weak landing page. Six habits cause most of the waste.

  • Putting every appliance into one campaign.
  • Skipping negative keywords for parts, manuals and training.
  • Not tracking phone calls as conversions.
  • Judging results by clicks instead of booked jobs.
  • Sending clicks to a home page that never mentions the appliance.
  • Running ads when nobody can answer the phone.

Fixing the first three costs only time. Fixing the last three costs a better landing page and a calendar habit, which pay back on every dollar of ad spend afterward.

How do you turn these appliance repair PPC tips into a plan?

Pick three tips for week one, add two in month one and review at 30, 60 and 90 days. Do not start all 10 at once.

Step 1, week one: tips 1, 2 and 3. Split the campaigns, block junk searches and track calls.

Step 2, month one: tips 5 and 6. Name the appliance in every ad and send clicks to a matching page.

Step 3, days 30, 60 and 90: tip 8. Read the search terms, cut the weakest keyword group and repeat the best one.

Here is how to judge the first review. If a campaign has spent a full month and booked jobs, keep it and raise the budget a little. If it brought calls that do not book, fix the keywords and negatives. If it brought no calls, fix the ad and the page before you touch the budget.

How much should an appliance repair company spend on PPC?

Work backward from your job value. Divide your monthly ad budget by your target cost per booked job to see how many jobs it must book. As an example, a $2,000 budget with a $200 target needs 10 booked jobs. Adjust after a month of real data.

Does PPC work for appliance repair?

It can, because people with a broken appliance search when they need help. It works best with separate campaigns per appliance, blocked junk searches, tracked calls and a landing page for each appliance. Without those, clicks often come from parts and manual searches.

What negative keywords should appliance repair companies use?

Start with terms from people who do not want a repair visit, such as manual, parts, diy, jobs, training and free. Google says too many negatives can reduce your reach, so add them slowly. Review the search terms report weekly and add only words that wasted money.

What is Quality Score in Google Ads?

Quality Score is a diagnostic Google uses to rate keywords on expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing page experience. Treat it as a guide for fixing ads and pages, not a goal. Booked jobs and cost per booked job matter more than the score itself.
